readerTitle: Why Tesla's first car was a $100,000 sports car
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Tesla의 2006년 'Master Plan') + 실제 연구 (Ryan & Gross 하이브리드 옥수수 연구, Rogers, Moore) + 가상 적용 (누수 센서 배관업체, 세제 유통업체)
insight: 새로운 제품은 '모두'가 아니라 문제를 가장 절실히 느끼고 불완전함을 감수하는 소수에게 먼저 판다. 다만 그 소수의 열광은 주류 고객의 반응을 예고하지 않는다.
misconception: 새 제품은 처음부터 최대한 많은 사람에게 알려야 한다. 초기 고객이 열광하면 시장 전체가 따라온다.

sources.text: Musk, E. (2006). The Secret Tesla Motors Master Plan (just between you and me). Tesla blog.
Ryan, B. & Gross, N. C. (1943). The diffusion of hybrid seed corn in two Iowa communities. Rural Sociology, 8(1), 15–24.
Rogers, E. M. (1962). Diffusion of Innovations. Free Press.
Moore, G. A. (1991). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness.
배관업체와 세제 유통업체 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Musk의 'Master Plan' 블로그 글은 2006년 8월 게시. 당시 Musk는 회장(chairman)이었고 CEO는 2008년부터. 카드의 세 단계 요약이 원문과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
Roadster 가격은 모델·연도별로 약 $98,000~$109,000. 카드에는 'around $100,000'으로 적었습니다. 출시 연도: Roadster 2008년 인도 시작, Model S 2012년, Model 3 2017년.
Ryan & Gross 연구: 아이오와 두 지역, 하이브리드 옥수수 1920년대 말~1930년대 보급, 1940년대 초 거의 모든 농가가 채택, 초기 채택자들이 밭 일부에 먼저 시험 재배했다는 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요.
Rogers의 채택자 비율(혁신자 2.5%, 초기 채택자 13.5%, 초기 다수 34%, 후기 다수 34%, 지체자 16%)은 정규분포 표준편차로 정의한 이론적 구분입니다. 실측치가 아니라는 점을 카드 표현에서 유지하세요.
가상 사례 수치($250 설치비, 고객 500명, 매장 30곳)는 모두 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Why Tesla's first car was a $100,000 sports car
body: Tesla's first car was not a family car. It was a two-seat electric sports car that cost around $100,000, with limited range and few places to charge.
That wasn't a mistake. It was the plan, written down in public before the car existed.

image.label: A small sports car leading a line of ordinary family cars
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 2인승 스포츠카 한 대가 앞서 달리고, 뒤로 점점 평범한 세단과 소형차들이 길게 줄지어 따라옴. 실제 자동차 브랜드 로고, 엠블럼, 특정 차종 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who should buy your leak sensors first?
body: Your plumbing company has a new service: small sensors under sinks and by the water heater that text the homeowner, and you, the moment they detect water. Installation is $250. The app is basic and setup takes an hour.
You have budget for one first push. Who do you sell to first?

options.text: Every homeowner in your area, with a big local ad campaign
options.feedback: You reach the most people, but most don't feel this problem yet and will judge a rough product harshly. You pay to reach people who won't buy.

options.text: Homeowners who had water damage last year, and owners of holiday homes that sit empty
options.feedback: They already feel the pain, so they'll pay and forgive the basic app. You give up reach for buyers who actually buy and tell you what to fix.

options.text: Your 500 existing customers, free for the first month
options.feedback: Warm and easy, but free mostly attracts the curious. You learn little about who would pay $250.

cards.title: Step one: build a sports car.
body: In 2006, Elon Musk, then Tesla's chairman, published a short blog post called the "Secret Master Plan." Build a sports car. Use that money to build an affordable car. Use that money to build an even more affordable car.
The Roadster went to drivers who wanted an electric car badly enough to accept the price, the short range and the lack of chargers.
Their money and feedback helped pay for what came next: the Model S in 2012 and the cheaper Model 3 in 2017.

image.label: Three steps: sports car, sedan, smaller car, each with a lower price tag
image.brief: 계단 세 칸 인포그래픽. 첫 칸에 작은 스포츠카와 큰 가격표, 둘째 칸에 세단과 중간 가격표, 셋째 칸에 소형차와 작은 가격표. 화살표로 '돈과 피드백'이 다음 칸으로 흐르는 모습. 실제 로고·차종 디자인 금지.

cards.title: Early adopters
body: **Early adopters** are the small group of customers who take up a new product before most people do. They feel the problem strongly, like being first, and will put up with a product that is expensive or unfinished.
Tesla didn't try to convince every driver. It started with the few who already wanted what it could build. Your best leak-sensor buyers are the same: people who have already had a flood.
cards.softwareNote: Early adopters often show up as beta users or *design partners* who use an unfinished product in return for regular feedback. A dozen who use it weekly teach you more than thousands of sign-ups who never return.

cards.title: Iowa farmers and hybrid corn
body: In the 1930s, hybrid seed corn promised bigger harvests. Sociologists Bryce Ryan and Neal Gross studied how farmers in two Iowa communities took it up. A few switched early, often testing it on part of a field first. Most waited years, watching neighbors' results. By the early 1940s, almost all had switched.
Everett Rogers later built on studies like this. His model sorts adopters into groups: innovators, **early adopters**, an early and a late majority, and laggards.

image.label: Bell curve of adoption split into five groups
image.brief: 종 모양 곡선을 다섯 구간으로 나눈 인포그래픽. 왼쪽부터 "Innovators 2.5%", "Early adopters 13.5%", "Early majority 34%", "Late majority 34%", "Laggards 16%". 두 번째 구간만 강조색. 작은 옥수수밭 일러스트를 배경에 은은하게.

cards.title: Early adopters are not a preview of everyone.
body: Early adopters buy a promise. Most customers buy proof. In his 1991 book *Crossing the Chasm*, Geoffrey Moore called the gap between them a **chasm**. Mainstream buyers want a finished, reliable product, a fair price and references from people like them.
So early excitement doesn't mean the market will follow. Early adopters can also cost you: they ask for custom changes and may leave for the next new thing.

cards.title: Now it's a detergent distributor.
body: You distribute a new laundry detergent sold as dry sheets, with no plastic bottle. Thirty zero-waste shops stock it and reorder every month.
A regional supermarket chain is interested, but its buyer wants proof it will sell in their stores. What do you do?

options.text: Show the reorder numbers as proof and push for a chain-wide launch
options.feedback: Fast growth if it works. But zero-waste shoppers are early adopters, and a flop across every store could end the relationship.

options.text: Propose a trial in a few stores, with clearer packaging and a price next to regular detergent
options.feedback: Slower, but you test what mainstream shoppers do and earn the proof the buyer needs. It treats early sales as a start, not a forecast.

options.text: Stay with zero-waste shops, where customers love it
options.feedback: Safe and loyal, but small. You keep your best fans and give up the larger market without ever testing it.

cards.title: Sell first to those who need it most, then earn the rest.
body: Start with the few who feel the problem most and forgive rough edges. Learn from them, then rebuild for the mainstream, which wants proof, not promise.
**Try it today:** list the ten customers who would be most upset if your newest product disappeared. What do they have in common?
